plates.title: Recorded enrolment fell when the count moved to individual student records
plates.sub: Pupils enrolled in recognised schools, pre-primary to class 12, each academic year; the sum of the state counts.
plates.explain: Until 2021-22 schools reported their totals. From 2022-23 every pupil is a separate record, which the Ministry says removed duplicate entries, so the two stretches are different rulers. Part of the fall at the switch is a cleaner count.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+, via MoSPI eSankhyiki

plates.title: Fewer pupils stay on after class 8
plates.sub: Pupils enrolled at each stage of school.
plates.explain: Primary covers five classes, upper primary three, and secondary and higher secondary two each, so compare per class. These are different children at each stage this year, not one group followed over time.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+ existing structure report, Table 1

plates.title: Enrolment falls away at higher secondary, most for Scheduled Tribe children
plates.sub: Gross enrolment ratio: pupils at each stage as a share of the children of the official age for it.
plates.explain: A gross ratio counts pupils of any age, so it can pass 100 when older children are still in lower classes. Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe ratios use their own child populations.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+ existing structure report, Table 1

plates.title: Girls are close to half the pupils at every stage, and just over half at higher secondary
plates.sub: Girls as a share of pupils enrolled at each stage, all school types.
plates.explain: A share near half reflects the number of girls and boys of school age as well as enrolment. Gender gaps in access are clearer in the state-by-state gender ratios in Every Cut.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+, via MoSPI eSankhyiki

plates.title: Higher-secondary enrolment varies widely across states
plates.sub: Gross enrolment ratio at higher secondary, classes 11 and 12, in each state and union territory.
plates.explain: Each state is measured against its own population aged 16 and 17. Children who cross a state border to study raise one state’s ratio and lower another’s, which is how a small territory can pass 100.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+, via MoSPI eSankhyiki

rows.name: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu

plates.title: Fewer than half of those who start class 1 are still in school at class 12
plates.sub: Retention: pupils reaching the last class of each cycle, as a share of those who started class 1.
plates.explain: Retention compares enrolment at the end of a cycle with the matching starting class. It is estimated from enrolment counts, not by following individual children, and it includes children who left and came back.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+ existing structure report, Table 1

plates.title: The hardest step is from class 10 to class 11
plates.sub: Transition: pupils in the last class of one stage who enrol in the first class of the next, the following year.
plates.explain: Transition is measured at the doors between stages. Pupils who move to vocational courses or to schools outside the system count as not having moved on.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+ existing structure report, Table 1

plates.title: Secondary dropout rates differ sharply across states
plates.sub: Dropout rate in classes 9 and 10, in each state and union territory.
plates.explain: The rate is estimated from enrolment in successive years, so migration and changes in reporting move it too. A published zero can come from that arithmetic and rounding.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+, via MoSPI eSankhyiki

rows.name: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu

plates.title: Government runs most schools but teaches only about half the pupils
plates.sub: Each management type’s share of schools, of pupils and of teachers.
plates.explain: Government schools are many and small; private unaided schools are fewer and larger. Other covers the schools the report does not place in the three main groups.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+ existing structure report, Table 1

plates.title: Higher secondary has the most pupils per teacher
plates.sub: Pupils enrolled per teacher at each stage.
plates.explain: This is an average over all schools. A good national ratio can sit beside crowded classrooms in one place and nearly empty ones in another, and it says nothing about whether teachers are present.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+ existing structure report, Table 1

plates.title: Many schools still run with a single teacher
plates.sub: Schools with only one teacher, and the pupils enrolled in them; the sum of the state counts.
plates.explain: A single teacher may have to teach several classes at once and also run the school. Most of these are small primary schools in villages.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+, via MoSPI eSankhyiki

plates.title: Water and toilets are nearly everywhere; computers, internet and accessible toilets lag
plates.sub: Schools reporting each facility, as a share of schools.
plates.explain: A facility counts if the school reports having it, whether or not it works every day. Boys’ and girls’ toilets are measured against the schools that need them.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+ existing structure report, Table 1

plates.title: Not every toilet or connection that exists works
plates.sub: Schools with each facility, and schools where it works; the sum of the state counts.
plates.explain: The gap between the two bars is schools where the toilet or electricity connection exists but is out of use.
plates.source: Ministry of Education, UDISE+, via MoSPI eSankhyiki

plates.title: Village pupils mostly study in government schools; town pupils mostly do not
plates.sub: Where enrolled pupils study, by type of school, rural and urban.
plates.explain: From the household survey of April to June 2025, which asked families where each child studies.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 80 Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education

plates.title: A private unaided school costs families many times a government one
plates.sub: Average spending per pupil in the academic year, by type of school, in rupees.
plates.explain: This counts what the family spent on the child’s schooling: fees, books, uniform, transport and other items. Private coaching is counted separately, in the last two charts.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 80 Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education

plates.title: The school bill rises with each stage
plates.sub: Average spending per pupil in the academic year, by stage, in rupees.
plates.explain: An average over all pupils at the stage, in every type of school. It rises partly because more older pupils study in private schools.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 80 Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education

plates.title: Course fees are the largest part of the school bill
plates.sub: Average spending per pupil in the academic year, by item, in rupees.
plates.explain: These items add up to the total bill. Many pupils pay no course fee at all, so the fee average mixes those who pay a lot with those who pay nothing.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 80 Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education

plates.title: Private coaching becomes common from secondary school
plates.sub: Pupils taking private coaching during the academic year, by stage, per cent.
plates.explain: Coaching here means paid tuition outside school, whether one-to-one or at a coaching centre.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 80 Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education

plates.title: For a pupil who takes coaching, the bill climbs steeply by higher secondary
plates.sub: Average coaching spending in the academic year per pupil who took coaching, by stage, in rupees.
plates.explain: This average is only over pupils who took coaching. Averaged over all pupils, coaching costs much less, because most pupils take none.
plates.source: MoSPI, NSS 80 Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education
